title: Planet Earth & Climate · Episode 3
chapters: Tornadoes: the most violent winds on Earth
Droughts and flooding rains: Australia's weather

units.t: Planet Earth & Climate. Episode three.
In this episode: Lightning: how storms make electricity, Tornadoes: the most violent winds on Earth, Monsoons: the seasons of rain and Droughts and flooding rains: Australia's weather.
Part one. Lightning: how storms make electricity.
Somewhere on Earth, lightning strikes dozens of times every second.
Here is how a cloud builds up enough electricity to light the sky, why thunder follows, and how to stay safe.
Hotter than the Sun.
In an instant, a channel of air only a few centimetres wide is heated to roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius, about five times hotter than the visible surface of the Sun.
Satellites suggest 40 to 50 flashes every second worldwide, over a billion a year.
Most are over tropical land, where warm, moist air rises fastest.
Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, where lake air meets cool mountain winds, is one of the most lightning-rich spots on Earth.
Central Africa's Congo basin is another, and Australia's tropical north has spectacular storms before the wet season, with Darwin famous for its evening light shows.
Lightning also helps life: its heat joins nitrogen and oxygen into compounds that rain carries into soil for plants to use.
Building the charge.
A thunderstorm is a giant vertical engine.
Warm, humid air rushes upward, cools and condenses into droplets, and near the top they freeze.
Inside, powerful updrafts throw around tiny ice crystals, supercooled water and soft ice pellets called graupel.
When crystals and graupel collide, electric charge is transferred.
The lighter crystals, generally positive, are swept to the top, while the heavier graupel, usually negative, gathers lower down.
The cloud becomes a giant battery, with opposite charges separated by kilometres of air.
Air is a good insulator, so charge keeps building until the insulation finally breaks down.
Exactly how a flash begins is still an active area of research.
Leader, stroke and thunder.
Most lightning never reaches the ground.
When a bolt does, it begins with a faint, branching channel of charged air, the stepped leader, zigzagging down.
Near the ground, tall objects send up streamers.
When they meet, the circuit is complete and the return stroke, the blinding flash we see, surges up into the cloud.
Several strokes often follow the same channel, making lightning flicker.
Thunder is the sonic boom.
The channel heats so fast that the air expands explosively, sending out a shock wave.
Distant thunder rumbles because sound from a long, twisting channel arrives at different times and echoes.
Sound travels about a third of a kilometre per second, so count the seconds from flash to thunder and divide by three for the distance in kilometres.
Myths that can hurt you.
Several popular beliefs about lightning are wrong.
It does strike the same place twice.
Tall buildings are hit again and again, and the Empire State Building is struck many times every year.
Rubber tyres do not make a car safe.
A hard-topped car protects you because its metal body carries the current around the outside and into the ground, keeping the people inside out of its path.
Lying flat on the ground is poor advice, because current can spread across the surface.
Sheltering under a lone tree is one of the worst choices of all: the tree is a likely target, and the current can jump sideways to anyone standing beneath it.
Staying safe in a storm.
The simplest rule is 'when thunder roars, go indoors'.
If you can hear thunder, the storm is close enough for lightning to reach you, because strikes can land many kilometres from the main storm.
The safest places are solid buildings with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped vehicle with the windows up.
Inside, avoid corded phones, running water and touching plugged-in appliances, since current can travel through wiring and pipes.
Experts generally suggest waiting around 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back outside.
This is general information, not personal advice.
In severe weather, check Bureau of Meteorology warnings and follow your state emergency service's instructions.
The key idea: A lightning bolt heats a narrow channel of air to several times the Sun's surface temperature, and it strikes constantly.
Part two. Tornadoes: the most violent winds on Earth.
Tornadoes produce the fastest winds measured near the ground, yet they are small, brief and still not fully understood.
Here is what we do know.
Born in supercells.
A tornado is a column of rapidly spinning air touching both the ground and the base of a thunderstorm.
Many show as a funnel because falling pressure condenses moisture and dust thickens the shape.
Most last a few minutes and travel a few kilometres, but a few become monsters, hundreds of metres wide and tens of kilometres long.
The powerful ones form in supercells.
Warm, moist air near the ground, cooler, drier air above, a lifting trigger and wind shear, winds changing speed and direction with height, set the lower atmosphere rolling horizontally.
A strong updraft tilts that roll upright, so the updraft rotates.
This broad column is a mesocyclone.
Why only some supercells produce tornadoes is still being researched.
Tornado Alley.
The United States records on the order of a thousand or more tornadoes in a typical year, far more than any other country.
Warm, humid air flows north from the Gulf of Mexico, dry air descends from the Rockies and south west deserts, and cold air sweeps down from Canada.
They meet over flat plains, with no east to west mountain range to keep them apart.
The region from Texas to South Dakota is nicknamed Tornado Alley, and the south east sees many deadly tornadoes too.
The Tri-State Tornado of 1925 killed nearly 700 people across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana.
Bangladesh, however, suffered the deadliest tornado on record, in 1989.
Measuring the unmeasurable.
Ordinary instruments are usually destroyed by a tornado, or simply not in the right place.
In 1971 the meteorologist Ted Fujita created a scale that estimated wind speed from the damage left behind.
The United States replaced it in 2007 with the Enhanced Fujita scale, which runs from EF0, peeling shingles and breaking branches, to EF5, where well built houses are swept off their foundations.
EF5 winds are estimated at over 320 kilometres per hour.
Portable Doppler radar has since let scientists chase storms and measure winds inside them.
During the Oklahoma outbreak of May 1999, a truck-mounted radar recorded winds of around 480 kilometres per hour, among the highest ever measured on Earth.
Tornadoes in Australia.
Many Australians are surprised to learn tornadoes happen here.

They are reported every year, most often in the south west of Western Australia, along the eastern seaboard and in parts of inland New South Wales and Queensland, and some are spawned by tropical cyclones coming ashore.
Most are short-lived and weak, but destructive ones occur, such as the tornado that tore through Bucca in Queensland in 1992.
A common confusion is worth clearing up.
The 'willy-willy' of outback folklore is usually a dust devil, a spinning column of air that forms on hot, clear days from heated ground, not from a storm.
Dust devils are mostly harmless curiosities, while true tornadoes need a thunderstorm overhead.
Staying safe.
Take warnings seriously.
In Australia, follow the Bureau of Meteorology's severe thunderstorm warnings, and call 000 in a life-threatening emergency.
If a tornado approaches, go to the lowest floor of a sturdy building and into a small interior room, such as a bathroom or hallway, with as many walls as possible between you and the outside.
Stay away from windows, and cover your head and neck.
Cars and caravans offer poor protection.
One old myth deserves retiring.
People were once told to open windows so the house would not explode from low pressure.
In fact, houses are destroyed by wind and flying debris, and time spent opening windows is time not spent sheltering.
The key idea: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air from a storm cloud to the ground, and the strongest come from supercells.
Part three. Monsoons: the seasons of rain.
For billions of people, the most important weather event of the year is the arrival of the monsoon.
Its rains decide harvests, rivers and even history.
More than rain.
The word monsoon comes, through Portuguese and Dutch, from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season.
People often use it to mean heavy rain, but strictly a monsoon is a pattern of winds that reverses direction with the seasons.
For part of the year, winds blow in from the ocean, carrying moisture and bringing a long wet season.
For the rest, they blow from the land, bringing dry weather.
Monsoons affect South Asia, East and South East Asia, West Africa, northern Australia and parts of the Americas.
The South Asian monsoon is the largest and most famous, and it shapes the lives and livelihoods of well over a billion people.
How the engine works.
The basic driver is simple.
Land heats and cools much faster than the ocean.
In late spring and summer the land warms strongly, and the hot air above it rises, creating lower pressure near the ground.
Cooler, moist air flows in from the ocean to replace it.
As that humid air is lifted, by heating or by mountains, it cools and drops its moisture as rain.
In winter the pattern reverses, as the land becomes cooler than the sea.
The real picture is more complicated.
The monsoon is also tied to the seasonal migration of the tropical rain belt, the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which follows the Sun's strongest heating north and south through the year.
India's great monsoon.
Each year the India Meteorological Department watches for the monsoon to arrive on the coast of Kerala, at India's southern tip, typically around 1 June.
Over the following weeks the rains push north and usually cover almost the whole country by early to mid-July.
The South West monsoon delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rainfall in just four months.
The Himalaya and the high Tibetan Plateau play a crucial role.
The plateau heats strongly in summer, helping power the circulation, while the mountains keep the moisture over the subcontinent.
A good monsoon fills reservoirs, recharges groundwater and feeds rice and other crops.
A weak one can mean drought, falling harvests and rising food prices.
The wettest places on Earth.
Some of the wettest places on Earth are in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, in north east India.
Monsoon winds loaded with moisture from the Bay of Bengal are forced up steep slopes and wring out torrential rain.
The village of Mawsynram averages close to 12 metres of rain a year, among the highest averages anywhere.
Nearby Cherrapunji holds a famous record: in the twelve months from August 1860 to July 1861 it received more than 26 metres.
People have adapted in remarkable ways.
Some Khasi villages have grown living bridges by training the roots of rubber fig trees across rivers over many years, creating structures that grow stronger with age.
Trade and Australia's monsoon.
Because monsoon winds blow reliably one way for part of the year and the other way later, a ship could sail across the Arabian Sea and return when the winds reversed.
Arab, Indian, Persian, African, and later Greek and Roman merchants used this to trade spices, pepper, textiles, gems and gold between East Africa, Arabia, India and South East Asia.
A first century Greek guidebook, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes these routes.
Australia has a monsoon too.
Across the Top End, the Kimberley and Cape York, the wet season runs roughly November or December to March, with north westerly winds, heavy rain and humidity, arriving in active bursts and breaks.
First Nations peoples of the north recognise many more seasons than two, based on detailed knowledge of weather, plants and animals.
The key idea: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings a wet season and a dry season, and the word means season.
Part four. Droughts and flooding rains: Australia's weather.
Why Australia swings between drought and flood, and what El Niño and La Niña actually mean.
Why so dry.
Dorothea Mackellar's 1908 poem My Country described 'a land of sweeping plains...
of droughts and flooding rains'.
She was right.
Australia is the driest inhabited continent, and its rainfall varies more from year to year than almost anywhere else.
Long droughts, like the Millennium Drought from about 1997 to 2009, can be broken by devastating floods, like those in Queensland in 2010-11.
Much of Australia lies between about 20 and 35 degrees south, where sinking dry air creates belts of high pressure, the same kind of belt that makes the Sahara and Kalahari.
High pressure means clear skies.
The land is also flat, with few mountains to force moist air upwards, and the interior is far from the sea.
So about 70 per cent is arid or semi-arid, and most people live near the wetter coast.
El Niño and La Niña.
The biggest driver of year-to-year rainfall in eastern Australia is the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, a pattern in the tropical Pacific Ocean.
Normally, trade winds pile warm water near Australia and Indonesia, which fuels rain clouds.
During El Niño, the winds weaken and warm water spreads east towards South America.
The rain moves with it, so eastern Australia often gets drier conditions, hotter days and higher bushfire risk.
La Niña is the opposite.
Stronger trade winds pile even more warm water near Australia, bringing more evaporation, cloud and rain to eastern and northern Australia, and a higher chance of floods and cyclones.
Three La Niña years in a row from 2020 to 2022 brought record floods to parts of New South Wales and Queensland.
Indian Ocean and Southern Ocean.
The Indian Ocean has its own pattern, the Indian Ocean Dipole, or IOD: a difference in sea temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean.
In a positive IOD, cooler water near Australia means less moisture and often drier conditions for southern and central Australia in winter and spring.
A negative IOD tends to bring more rain.
In 2019 a strong positive IOD helped bring the extreme drought and heat behind the Black Summer bushfires.
The Southern Annular Mode describes the movement of the westerly winds circling Antarctica.
When they and their cold fronts shift south, southern Australia gets less winter rain.
When they shift north, more storms reach Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth.
The westerlies have tended to sit further south in recent decades, contributing to declining winter rainfall in south-west Western Australia.
Bushfire weather.
Bushfires need fuel, dry conditions, heat and wind, plus an ignition source like lightning.
Wet La Niña years can grow extra grass and scrub, which then dries out and provides more fuel.
Hot, dry winds ahead of cold fronts create the most dangerous fire weather.
Australia's Fire Danger Rating system, updated in 2022, has four levels: Moderate, High, Extreme and Catastrophic.
The Black Summer fires of 2019-20 burned more than 24 million hectares.
Climate change is making dangerous fire weather more frequent.
Reading the forecast.

The Bureau of Meteorology monitors ENSO, the IOD and the Southern Annular Mode, and publishes long-range outlooks showing the chances of wetter or drier, warmer or cooler conditions over the coming months.
These help farmers decide what to plant, water authorities plan storage and emergency services prepare.
For everyday life, it's worth knowing your local risks, whether flood, fire, cyclone or heat.
Have an emergency plan, and follow warnings through the official apps of your state emergency services.
The key idea: Australia is the driest inhabited continent, with rainfall that swings between drought and flood.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Where is lightning most common?
Answer. Over tropical land, where warm air rises.
Question two. What is a mesocyclone?
Answer. A rotating updraft in a supercell storm.
Question three. Strictly speaking, what is a monsoon?
Answer. Winds that reverse with the seasons.
Question four. Why is so much of Australia dry?
Answer. Sinking dry air, flat land and few mountains.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
